title: Ignatian imagination
hookLine: Ignatius of Loyola taught people to pray by stepping into a gospel scene

lines: A DUSTY ROAD, A TIRED COUPLE.
cards: Where do you stand when you hear a gospel story? A dusty road. A pregnant young woman is riding, and a man walks beside her, tired, looking ahead for somewhere to stop for the night.
There's a servant with them, carrying what they own. Then you notice the servant is you. You're carrying the bag.
Your feet hurt. You can hear the animal breathing. This is a set of instructions for prayer, from a Spanish soldier turned seeker named Ignatius of Loyola, who went on to found the Jesuits.
Yesterday's book put every image down. Today's teacher picks them all up, and walks in.

teach.b: You met Ignatius's nightly examen on day one hundred eight. His handbook, the Spiritual Exercises, is a guide for a retreat, usually given by one person to another, and here's how its imagining works.

First, build the place. Before praying with a gospel story, Ignatius asks the person to see the setting with the eye of the imagination: how long the road is, how wide, whether it's flat or runs through valleys.
He calls this composing the place. It's how the mind stops wandering and arrives somewhere.

teach.h: FIND THE PEOPLE, AND FIND YOURSELF.
teach.b: Second, find the people, and find yourself.
In his exercise on the birth of Jesus, he asks the one praying to watch Mary, Joseph, and a servant girl, and to become a small, unworthy servant among them, helping with what they need.
Third, use every sense. Later in the day, Ignatius suggests going back over the same scene sense by sense: what you see, what you hear, what you might smell and taste, what you'd touch.
Readers call this the application of the senses.

teach.h: THEN SPEAK, AS FRIEND TO FRIEND.
teach.b: Fourth, then talk. Ignatius ends with a conversation, speaking as one friend speaks to another, telling what's on your heart and asking for what you need.

The imagination is the door: the scene gets you close enough to speak. Some who pray this way say the story becomes a place they can visit, and that a sore foot or a cold wind does more than a perfect picture.

how: Christians who pray in the Ignatian way often take a gospel passage, read it slowly, then enter the scene in imagination and end by talking with Jesus; it is commonly practiced on guided retreats with a spiritual director.

games.q: you're praying Ignatius's exercise on the birth of Jesus. where does he put you?
o: high above, watching the whole country.
among them, as a small servant helping.
in Mary's place, telling the story.
games.why: Ignatius asks the one praying to become a small, unworthy servant among Mary, Joseph and the others, helping with what they need.

practice: Choose a short scene: if you pray with the Bible, the road to Bethlehem or a fishing boat at dawn; if not, any story that matters to you.

Build the place, find where you stand among the people, and notice one sound, one smell, one thing your hand touches. Near the end, if you pray, speak to someone in the scene, plainly; if not, notice what it stirs.

wordCard.voice: Ignatian imagination. Praying by stepping into a story: build the place, find yourself in it, use the senses, then speak. From the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: step into the scene. Close enough to speak. Same time tomorrow.
